# About this book {.unnumbered}

In 1898 Albert Michelson built a machine that adds twenty sine waves together
using gears, cams, springs and levers, and draws the result with a pen. Turn
the crank and it performs Fourier synthesis. Turn it the other way — set up
differently — and it performs Fourier analysis, the operation Michelson himself
called too mathematical to explain.

One of these machines survives in a glass case at the University of Illinois.
There has never been a plan for building one.

This book is that plan: every part, every setup, every cut, on a manual mill
and a lathe.

::: {.callout-important}
## Verification policy

Current Book workstream status and sequencing live in the
[Harmonic Analyzer project](https://github.com/users/pedropaulovc/projects/1).
Each chapter's `status:` frontmatter records its maturity. Chapters may be
drafted from CAD, but a chapter is `verified` only after the part has been made
by following its text.
:::

## What comes with it

The CAD model, the neutral STEP exports, the drawing sheets and the interactive
simulator are open source, MIT-licensed, and free whether or not you buy this
book:

- **[github.com/pedropaulovc/harmonic-analyzer](https://github.com/pedropaulovc/harmonic-analyzer)**

## Acknowledgements

This project would not exist without Bill Hammack, Steve Kranz and Bruce
Carpenter, whose book *Albert Michelson's Harmonic Analyzer: A Visual Tour of a
Nineteenth Century Machine that Performs Fourier Analysis* (Articulate Noise
Books, 2014) and the accompanying engineerguy video series rescued this machine
from obscurity, photographed it beautifully, and explained it clearly. Their
